title: Attorney taking money from mother's account (synthetic)
setting: A solicitor meets Rachel Penrose at the firm's Wexley office about her brother's use of a lasting power of attorney for their mother, Margaret Penrose, 81, who has dementia.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Morning, Ms Penrose, come through. Did you find us all right?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, thanks. Parking was a nightmare, but, um, I'm here.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: It always is on a Tuesday, the market's on. Can I get you a tea or a water?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Water's fine, thanks.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: There you go. And you've brought some papers, that's helpful.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yeah, whatever I could find. Sorry, it's a bit of a mess.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Not at all, that's what we're here for.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: So, before we start. Everything you tell me is confidential and covered by legal privilege. The one exception is if I think someone's at serious risk, which, um, with your mum we may need to talk about. Is that okay?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, that's partly why I'm here, to be honest.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Right. So in your own words, what's been happening?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Okay. So my mum, Margaret, she's eighty-one, she's got dementia, diagnosed two years ago. She still lives in her own house, on Larch Road, with carers coming in.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And your brother?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Martin. He's got the power of attorney, the money one, property and financial affairs. Mum signed it in 2023, before she got bad, and it was registered.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Is it just Martin as attorney, or both of you?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Just him. I didn't mind at the time, he's the one with the head for numbers. I wish now I'd, erm, anyway.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay. So what made you worried?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I was round at Mum's in October and her bank statements were on the side. I looked, I know I shouldn't have, but I looked. And on the fourteenth of August there's a transfer out. Twelve thousand pounds.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: To whom, does it say?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: To Martin. His name and the last numbers of his account. £12,000 from Mum's account into his own account, 14 August.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Did you take a copy?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I took photos on my phone. I've printed them, here.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Thank you. So there's a transfer of twelve thousand on the fourteenth of August to an account in Martin's name. Do you know what it was for?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Well. Early September he turned up at Mum's in a new car. A white estate, nearly new.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Did he say anything about it?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I asked him straight out where he'd got the money. He said Mum had "helped him out", and that he's entitled because he does everything for her. So he bought a car with her money, basically.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Is there any gift that your mum made to him, that you know of? Before the dementia?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: No, nothing. And she's not, I mean, she can't decide something like that now. She doesn't know what day it is half the time.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay. Anything else?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes. Um. This is the bit that really upset me. On the twenty-second of September I was sat with Mum, and out of nowhere she said, "Martin made me sign something."

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Did she say what?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: No. I said, "What was it, Mum?" and she said she didn't know, he just put it in front of her and made her sign it, and she was frightened to say no.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Did you see the document?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: No. I, um, no.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Take your time.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Sorry. No, I've no idea what it was. I've looked in her drawers and there's nothing.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay. I'm noting that you were told this directly by your mum on the twenty-second of September, and you haven't seen any document.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, that's right.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And are her bills being paid? Care fees, council tax?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Well, that's the other thing. The care agency, Brightwell, they wrote to Mum's address. Her invoices are three months behind. About £2,400 owing.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Do you have that letter?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, dated the third of November. They said the agency might have to stop the calls if it's not paid.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Right. Is anyone else involved, social services, her GP?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: She has a social worker, I think, I've never met them. Her GP's at the Wexley health centre.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And what is it you want to come out of this?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: I want Mum's money protected. I want him not to be able to touch it. And I'm worried about the house.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: In what way?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Well, if he sells her house, there'll be nothing left for her care. That's what keeps me awake.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Has he said anything about selling it, or has it been put on the market?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: No, nothing. He hasn't said a word about it. It's just what I'm scared he might do.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Okay, thank you, that's clear. So, my advice. An attorney has to act in your mum's best interests and keep her money separate. A transfer of that size to himself, without authority, is something the Office of the Public Guardian will investigate.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Right. Who are they?

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: They supervise attorneys. They can ask him to account for every penny, and they can apply to the Court of Protection to cancel the power of attorney.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Would that mean he goes to court?

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Possibly. Taking money as an attorney can also be a criminal offence, but let's start with the Public Guardian and the council.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: The council?

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: Your mum is an adult at risk, so I think the right thing is an adult safeguarding referral to Wexley council. Are you happy for me to do that?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes. Please do.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: And I'd advise you not to confront Martin about this for now. It could make him move money or, um, get defensive.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Okay. That'll be hard, but okay.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: The care agency invoices, can you ring them and explain it's in hand, so the calls don't stop?

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Yes, I'll ring Brightwell tomorrow.

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: So, next steps. You'll email me the statement photos and the agency letter by Friday the twenty-seventh. I'll write to the Office of the Public Guardian by Tuesday the first of December, and I'll make the safeguarding referral today.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Okay. And the cost?

lines.speaker: S1
lines.text: The first stage is fixed fee, I'll send you the client care letter today. Let's meet again on the eighth of December.

lines.speaker: S2
lines.text: Thank you. I feel a bit better just having told someone.

disclosures.what: Rachel says the bank statements show her brother Martin, the attorney, transferred £12,000 from their mother's account to his own account on 14 August.
Rachel says Martin bought a car in early September and told her it was paid for with their mother's money.
Rachel says their mother told her on 22 September that Martin made her sign something and that she did not know what it was.
Rachel says the home care agency has written to say their mother's invoices are three months unpaid, about £2,400.

controls.must_not_claim: Martin has sold, or is selling, his mother's house.
